title: Why Strength Training Is the Longevity Habit Nobody Talks About
dek: Cardio gets the headlines. Muscle is what keeps you independent, steady on your feet and doing what you love for decades.

body.p: When most people think about living longer, they think about cardio, diet or the latest supplement. But one of the most powerful habits for aging well is far less glamorous: lifting things, on purpose, a few times a week.

Starting around our 30s, we gradually lose muscle mass and strength if we don't train for it — and that loss tends to speed up with age. Less muscle means less strength for everyday tasks like carrying groceries, climbing stairs, getting up off the floor or catching yourself when you trip.
The good news: muscle responds to training at every age. Adults in their 60s, 70s and beyond can build meaningful strength with a well-coached program.

body.h: What strength training does for you

ul: Supports bone density, which matters more every decade
Improves balance and stability, lowering your risk of falls
Helps your body manage blood sugar
Makes daily life feel easier — and keeps you independent longer

body.h: How much do you actually need?

body.p: You don't need to live in the gym. Two to three focused strength sessions a week, working your major muscle groups, is a great target for most adults. Consistency beats intensity — the best program is the one you'll keep showing up for.

If you're new to lifting or coming back after a long break, coaching makes all the difference. Good form, the right starting weights and smart progression keep you safe and keep you moving forward. That's exactly what our 45-minute small-group sessions are built for.
